job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Omar Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my desk at Halden Freight by 8:15. I'm a procurement trainee, so I compare supplier quotes, chase delivery dates and update the purchase tracker. About half of that I run through an AI assistant now, and I check what it gives me. I rent a room in a shared house in Orrin with two others, and my student loan is 37,000. After work I read about markets and put 20 a week into an index fund, which sounds grand but it's tiny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the sensible outcome, and also a bit of a shame. At work I'd tell Greta, my team lead, we should keep using the tools for quotes and tracking and take the time saved for supplier calls. Online I'd just share the good tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay but impatient. I earn 23,200, and after rent and loan I invest 80 a month and have about 120 spare. If nothing changes, I'm on a slow climb up the ladder at Halden, and a slow climb with debt is a long climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and aim for a buyer's role in about 18 months. I'd keep investing the 20 a week, maybe raise it to 30. I'd ask Greta to put me on the bigger supplier contracts, so I get real numbers to work with. And I'd keep an eye on other freight and logistics firms in the region, as there aren't many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little flat. I like speed, and this is a slow future, though it's reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You invest 20 a week with 37,000 of debt. Why not pay the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair challenge. The loan rate is about 6 percent, and I'm hoping the index fund does more. It's a risk, and some of my friends think I'm daft. But I want the habit of investing, and I'd rather start small than start at 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the fund dropped 20 percent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would sting, but it's a small number. I'd keep putting money in, because it's cheaper when it drops. If I lost my job at the same time I'd stop, and I'd pull the money out. I'm not stubborn about it.

say: It's the sensible outcome and a bit of a **shame**.
I'd tell Greta (my team lead) to use tools for quotes and take the time for **supplier calls**.
think: I'm okay but **impatient**: 23,200 pay and about 120 spare after rent, loan and investing.
A slow climb with **debt** is a long climb.
do: Aim for a **buyer's role** in about 18 months.
Raise the index fund from 20 to **30 a week**.
Ask Greta for the bigger **supplier contracts** to get real numbers.
feel: Fine but a little **flat**; I like speed and this future is slow but reliable.
S0.quote: I'd rather start small than start at 30.
fieldNote: Takes a small **risk** on investing before the debt is cleared, in line with adaptive traits.
Would stop investing and **withdraw** if he lost his job.

steps.text: Keep updating the purchase tracker and aim for a buyer's role
Raise the index fund contribution from 20 to 30 a week
Ask Greta for bigger supplier contracts to test the AI assistant on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real shift and the people who use the tools well will do fine. I'd tell Greta we should automate the quote comparison and the tracker now and shift people to relationships. Online I'd write a short post on how I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my trainee job is mostly the stuff that gets automated, comparing, tracking and chasing. But I'm the one who already knows how to use it, which helps. I might actually be more valuable if I run the tools than if I do the old work. But I can't be sure the firm sees it like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a small demo that shows how much time the quote comparison saves, and pitch it to Greta. I'd ask to take on the supplier relationship work, which needs a person. I'd take a short course on supply chain analytics. And I'd move my investing up a notch, maybe 35 a week, because I'd want a larger cushion if the firm shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, a bit anxious. It's like standing at the edge of a wave and hoping you pick the right moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pitch a demo that cuts your own work. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, a bit. But if I don't pitch it, someone else will, and they'll get the credit. Greta's fair, and I think she'd back me. If she doesn't, I'd know where I stand and I could look elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Halden is most exposed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Colin, who's been doing the delivery bookings for 15 years by hand. He's lovely and slow with the tools. If they automate bookings, I think he's first. I'd offer to teach him, but I'd bet he'd refuse out of pride.

say: It's a real shift and people who use the tools well will do **fine**.
I'd tell Greta to **automate** quote comparison and move people to relationships.

do: Build a small **demo** showing the time saved and pitch it to Greta.
Ask to take on **supplier relationship** work and take a supply chain analytics course.
Raise investing to about **35 a week** for a larger cushion.
feel: **Interested**, a bit anxious, like standing at the edge of a wave.

fieldNote: Takes a **calculated** risk by automating his own tasks first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's huge and the speed is the issue. I'd tell my team to start thinking about what we do that a machine can't. I'd say governments need to move now on retraining and income support. Not in two years, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm in trouble, even though I'm good with the tools. If AI does almost any thinking work better and cheaper, then being good with AI isn't a skill, it's a toll booth that vanishes. I've got 37,000 of debt, one month of savings and no family help. That's a bad combination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to turn my skills into something quick and hands-on. I'd take any money-making job on the side, like setting up automations for small firms, since I know how. I'd pay off a chunk of the loan using every pound I make. I'd also look at physical jobs in freight, like warehouse supervision, because robots in that world come later. And I'd keep what I've invested, in case it grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pressure, mostly. But there's a flicker of excitement, which I feel guilty about. It's a huge thing to be alive for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your investments. Wouldn't you need the cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell if I had to, I'm not precious. But the sums are small, 800 in total, so they won't pay rent for long. The bigger thing is the side work. That's where the real cash would come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your housemates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's talk about rent and a cheaper place together, now, before it's urgent. One of them, Remy, works in an insurance call centre, so he's even more exposed than me. I'd rather we plan than panic.

say: That's huge and the **speed** is the issue.
Governments must act on retraining and **income support** now, not in two years.
think: Being good with AI isn't a skill, it's a **toll booth** that vanishes.
With 37,000 of debt and one month saved I'm in a **bad combination**.
do: Take **side work** setting up automations for small firms.
Look at **physical** freight jobs like warehouse supervision.
Put every extra pound against the **loan**.
feel: **Pressure**, with a guilty flicker of excitement at living through something this big.
S2.quote: Being good with AI isn't a skill, it's a toll booth that vanishes.
fieldNote: Even as a heavy **AI user** he doesn't think skill protects him.

steps.text: Set up AI automations for small firms on evenings
Apply for warehouse supervisor jobs at freight firms
Put every extra pound against the student loan
Plan a cheaper shared place with my housemates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to be smart about it. I'd tell people to learn the tools, build savings and not assume anything. I'd also say we need public training funds starting now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm in a decent place. In five years, I could be a buyer or a supply analyst on a good salary, clear the loan and have a pot of money. Then AGI hits, and I'd need to be doing something that's more about people and decisions. I'm more excited than scared, though I'm not calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a three-part plan. Part one: get promoted to buyer within two years and pay the loan down fast. Part two: invest 60 a week into an index fund once the loan's below 20,000. Part three: start a small consultancy helping local firms adopt AI. I'd also stay open to a change in direction, maybe into logistics operations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised. The nerves are there, but mostly I feel like I've got time to do things, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you drop the consultancy plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw AI firms selling it to those same small businesses directly, with no need for me. Then I'd focus on the job and the savings. I'd rather quit early than hang on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes if you get passed over for buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move. There are three firms nearby, and one is the freight arm of a bigger company that's hiring. I'd rather move for a better role than wait. Staying put because it's comfortable is how people end up stuck.

say: Five years is enough to be smart: learn the tools, build **savings**, assume nothing.
think: I'm in a decent place: buyer or analyst, loan cleared and a **pot** of money.
After AGI I need to do something about **people and decisions**.

fieldNote: Has **exit** rules for each plan, like dropping the consultancy if AI vendors take that market.

steps.text: Get promoted to buyer within two years or move to another freight firm

Start a small consultancy helping local firms adopt AI
Pay the loan down fast in the first two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. I'd tell friends to build skills and savings, and to take the time seriously. I'd also say don't let anyone pretend it's not coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be in good shape. By 32 I could have a senior role, no debt and a decent pot in the fund. I'd have time to build something of my own, maybe a small firm. The risk is complacency, thinking ten years is forever, when it's actually only a few career moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the buyer role, then a senior role at a bigger firm by about 26. I'd clear the loan by 27 and save a deposit. I'd build the consultancy slowly, with a couple of clients a year. I'd also study part time, maybe for an operations qualification. And I'd invest steadily, 70 or 80 a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. I'd feel almost guilty about how well it works out for me, compared with the two-year world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be one of the lucky ones with the habit of learning, and not everyone has that. Colin wouldn't, and others like him. I'd want to do something about that, like volunteering to teach tools to older workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the long window change your plans for housing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd buy. I'd aim for a small flat by 29 or 30. In the two-year world I wouldn't even look. Normal life depends so much on how much warning you get.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, so build skills and savings and take it seriously.
Don't let anyone pretend it's not **coming**.

The risk is **complacency**, because ten years is only a few career moves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, though I'd cope better than most. Even with the tools, there's no time to turn debt into safety. What would help is quick support for people who aren't as lucky as me, and training that pays you to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being comfortable with AI doesn't mean I'm relaxed about it. I'm just one of the few who can see where it's heading and try to plan.

headlineQuote: I'm just one of the few who can see where it's heading and try to plan.
portrait: **Omar** is 22, a business graduate working as a procurement trainee at a freight firm, renting a room in Orrin.
He owes **37,000**, saves almost nothing and invests 20 a week in an index fund anyway.
He is a centrist who uses AI **daily**, takes risks and plans every scenario with clear exit points.
He sees skill with AI as a **toll booth** that won't protect him if AGI arrives fast.
Warning time changes his mood from anxious to **calm**, and his plans from side work to a home.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture: even with good tool skills there is no time to turn his debt into safety.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **support** for people less lucky than him and training that pays while they retrain.
